articles.title: Alberta independence explained: Why Canada's oil province wants out and where Trump fits in
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Alberta, the Canadian province of oil fields, cowboy country and the snow-capped Rocky Mountains, is preparing to ask a question that would have sound.
articles.body: Alberta, the Canadian province of oil fields, cowboy country and the snow-capped Rocky Mountains, is preparing to ask a question that would have sounded almost unthinkable in mainstream Canadian politics a few years ago: Should it begin the process of leaving Canada?Next month, the country's fourth-largest province will vote on whether its government should start the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on whether Alberta should separate from Canada.A “yes” vote will not make Alberta an independent country. There will be no new border posts on the Trans-Canada Highway and Calgary will not suddenly become the capital of a new nation.The October 19 vote itself is non-binding. It would simply open the door to a much bigger constitutional and political fight. Elections Alberta says voters will be asked to choose between remaining a province of Canada and directing the government to begin the legal process required for a future binding referendum on separation.But even taking that first step would be a remarkable moment for a province that has spent decades complaining about Ottawa while remaining firmly inside the Canadian federation.Alberta is roughly the size of France and is home to Canada's biggest oil-producing industry. Its capital is Edmonton, while Calgary is its best-known metropolitan centre and one of the country's major business hubs.In 2025, Alberta hosted the G7 Leaders' Summit in Kananaskis, where world leaders gathered just over an hour from Calgary. US President Donald Trump attended the summit, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi was among the invited leaders.The province is landlocked. Its southern edge, however, is geographically closer to the American plains than to many of Canada's major cities, including Ottawa.And now there is another, rather conspicuous figure hovering over Alberta's debate: US President Donald Trump.In his second presidential term, Trump has repeatedly described Canada as a potential “51st State”. He has talked about the two countries' shared border, trade and resources, while Alberta's oil wealth makes the province particularly relevant to his America-first energy vision.Put it all together and Alberta finds itself at the centre of an unusual political mix: an old western Canadian grievance, a powerful oil industry, frustration with Ottawa and an American president who keeps looking north.A rich province with a long memoryAlberta has done remarkably well for itself over the years.According to a report cited by Jacobin, the province outpaced most of Canada in GDP growth during the 21st century. The Business Council of Alberta says Albertans generate more economic value per person than anywhere else in the country.Alberta's GDP per capita remains the highest among Canadian provinces, reflecting the outsized role its energy sector plays in the provincial economy.A large part of that prosperity comes from underground.Oil and gas accounted for 22% of Alberta's GDP in 2023, making the energy industry far more than just another sector of the economy. It has helped shape Alberta's identity, its politics and, increasingly, its relationship with the rest of Canada.That relationship has not always been comfortable.For years, many Albertans have felt that their province generates enormous economic value but has too little control over the policies governing it. Ottawa, in their view, collects federal revenues from a resource-rich Alberta while imposing rules that can make it harder to develop those same resources.The resentment sharpened during Justin Trudeau's time as prime minister.Pipeline battles, carbon pricing, environmental regulations and federal restrictions on energy projects became much more than individual policy disputes. In Alberta, they became shorthand for a larger complaint about Ottawa's power over the province.Beneath all of it was a question that has never completely disappeared from Alberta politics: if Alberta contributes so much to the national economy, supporters ask, why should decisions about its resources be made elsewhere?Oil is where the independence argument beginsTo understand Alberta separatism, follow the oil.Canada's crude industry is overwhelmingly concentrated in Alberta. The province's oil sands contain some of the world's largest hydrocarbon deposits, while its conventional oil and gas sector remains a major employer and source of government revenue.And there is an obvious customer waiting just south of the border.The US is by far the most important market for Canadian crude.That has created a peculiar relationship. Alberta is politically part of Canada, but its energy industry is deeply plugged into the US economy.For separatists, the question almost writes itself: if Alberta produces the oil and American refineries are among its biggest customers, why should Ottawa have the final say over how those resources are developed?That frustration has been a recurring feature of Alberta politics for decades.But there is a catch.Oil may be Alberta's greatest economic strength, but the industry also depends heavily on infrastructure and decisions beyond the province's borders. Pipelines cross jurisdictions. Ports are outside Alberta. Trade agreements involve Ottawa. Financial and monetary policy remains federal.Leaving Canada would not suddenly make those constraints disappear.It would replace them with a completely new set of negotiations.An independent Alberta would also have to confront questions that are largely settled today: what currency it would use, how Canada's debt and assets would be divided, what would happen to pensions and federal programmes, and what access it would have to Canada's existing trade agreements.And Alberta's geography would make those negotiations particularly important. The province sits between two G7 countries, Canada and the US, and an independent Alberta would have to build a relationship with both.The question would be just how much room it would have to manoeuvre.Also read | Smells like separatism: Oil-rich Alberta slipping from Thwadda Canada to America?The money behind the angerFederal money is another major source of grievance.Alberta has long complained that it contributes more to the Canadian federation than it gets back through some national programmes. Equalization, in particular, has become an emotional issue in the province.The political argument is straightforward: Alberta earns, Ottawa collects and other parts of Canada benefit.Premier Danielle Smith has herself used that language.In a February address, she said Albertans could no longer be expected to “subsidize the entire country through equalization and federal transfers”.The accounting, however, is more complicated.Alberta does not receive equalization payments, although it does receive federal health and social transfers. Equalization itself is funded from federal general revenues rather than direct payments made by individual provinces. Whether Alberta is a net contributor to the federation depends on how federal taxes, spending and national programmes are calculated.That argument has been going on for years.What has changed is that the grievance is now being folded into a much larger question: should Alberta have greater control over its own money, resources and policies?That is the kind of greater autonomy Smith has advocated.From 'Wexit' to the ballot boxThere was a time when Alberta separatism could be dismissed as a fringe idea.It even had its own catchy name: “Wexit” -- a western Canadian play on Brexit.There were rallies, online campaigns and plenty of anger directed at Ottawa. But the idea of actually leaving Canada remained far outside the centre of Alberta's political life.Now the question has reached the ballot.The latest push did not begin with Smith or her government. It came from a citizen-led campaign seeking to put the independence question directly before Albertans.The initiative gathered far more signatures than required. Elections Alberta says 286,593 signatures were submitted, of which 279,337 were counted as valid. The petition needed 177,732 signatures to qualify.The process, however, became tangled in a legal dispute, including questions over whether Indigenous treaty rights had been properly considered.The Alberta government subsequently pursued another route.Smith announced that a separation question would be put to voters on October 19.But look closely at the wording and it is much less dramatic than “Do you want Alberta to become independent?”Albertans are instead being asked whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or whether the government should “commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution” to hold a future binding referendum on whether Alberta should separate from Canada.A vote to begin the process would be the beginning, not the end, of a much longer debate.And reaching the ballot does not mean most Albertans currently support separation. A June Ipsos poll put support for independence at 19%, according to Reuters.That leaves a considerable gap between frustration with Ottawa and support for actually leaving Canada.Smith wants Alberta stronger -- but inside CanadaThat leaves Danielle Smith in an unusual political position.The Alberta premier has become one of Canada's strongest voices for provincial autonomy. But she has not endorsed separation.Quite the opposite.When she announced the referendum question, Smith made her own position clear: “I will therefore be voting for Alberta to remain in Canada.”She has described her preferred future as a “strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada”.Her argument, therefore, is not that Alberta should leave Canada. It is that Alberta should have considerably more power while remaining part of the federation.At the same time, she has accepted that the independence movement has become too significant to simply ignore.Her government has effectively opened the political door to a question separatists have been asking for years.Smith's reasoning is that Albertans should be able to settle the issue democratically rather than allowing the anger to keep building.In May, she said that “kicking the can down the road” would only prolong an emotional and important debate.That balancing act is at the heart of Alberta's current politics.Smith does not want to lead a separatist campaign.But she also does not want to be seen as shutting down Albertans who want to ask the question.A provincial vote cannot simply break up CanadaThis is where the political rhetoric runs into the Canadian Constitution.Even if Albertans eventually vote for independence, the province cannot simply declare itself a new country.Canada has already been through much of this debate with Quebec.The Supreme Court of Canada ruled on provincial secession in its Quebec reference, establishing that a province cannot unilaterally walk away from the federation.A clear majority voting in favour of secession on a clear question would instead create an obligation for the different parties in Canada to enter negotiations.The federal Clarity Act subsequently established a framework for determining whether the question and the majority are sufficiently clear.So even a successful independence referendum would lead to negotiations.And those negotiations would be anything but simple.There would be questions over Canada's debt and federal assets. There would be debates over borders, citizenship, pensions and trade. There would be questions about federal infrastructure and employees.Then there is perhaps the most complicated issue of all: Indigenous rights and treaties.Alberta is covered by Treaties 6, 7 and 8. Any attempt to change the province's constitutional status would therefore have to account for the rights of First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples.Smith acknowledged this when Alberta launched its Alberta Next process, saying any referendum would have to respect Indigenous rights and the treaty relationship.So there is no simple “independence” button waiting to be pressed.A vote would be the start of a long constitutional negotiation involving Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples.And then there is Donald TrumpIf Alberta's independence debate were simply a fight between Edmonton and Ottawa, it would already be a major Canadian political story.Trump has made it considerably more complicated.Since returning to the White House, Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state.He has complained about America's trade relationship with Canada, questioned the value of aspects of the bilateral relationship and repeatedly talked about the US-Canada border.At one point, Trump described the border as an “artificially drawn line”.That is not the sort of language Canadian politicians are accustomed to hearing from a US president.Trump has also made no secret of his interest in Canada's natural resources.His interest in Alberta is therefore difficult to separate from his broader “America First” approach to energy.For Alberta separatists, Trump's rhetoric provides an intriguing backdrop.Here is a US president repeatedly talking about Canada becoming part of the United States at almost exactly the same time Alberta is debating its place within Canada.But the two ideas are not the same.Alberta independence does not automatically mean AmericaTrump talks about the 51st state.Some Albertans talk about independence.Those are two very different propositions.Not every Alberta separatist wants the province to join the US. Some want an entirely independent Alberta. Others see closer integration with the US as attractive. And some support separation from Canada precisely because they want Albertans to make their own decisions.For that last group, swapping Ottawa for Washington would hardly be the point.The difference is fairly simple.Trump's argument is essentially that Canada would be better off inside the United States. The Alberta separatist argument is that Alberta could be better off outside Canada.One is annexation.The other is independence.The two ideas can overlap in political debate, but they are not the same project.Trump's words have become part of Alberta's debateTrump does not have to formally support Alberta independence to influence the conversation.Every mention of the “51st State” gives separatists another reason to talk about what an Alberta-US relationship might look like.But Trump's pressure on Canada also gives federalists a counterargument.If an independent Alberta became a small country sitting beside the world's largest economy, would that give it more leverage over Washington — or less?The question matters because Alberta's economic relationship with the US is already enormous.Much of its oil heads south. American refineries rely heavily on Canadian crude. Alberta's producers depend on access to the US market.That interdependence can look like an opportunity to separatists.It can also look like a vulnerability.Trump's trade policy has brought that vulnerability into sharper focus.The tariff questionTrump has repeatedly used tariffs as leverage against Canada.In August, a new round of 50% US tariffs took effect on specified Canadian products, adding another layer of tension to the trading relationship between the two countries. The measures have subsequently been adjusted for some product categories.The broader tariff dispute has affected around $20 billion worth of goods traded between the two countries, according to Reuters.For Alberta, that message lands differently from how it does in Ottawa.The province has an enormous commercial relationship with the US, but that relationship is ultimately governed through two national governments.An independent Alberta would have to negotiate its own relationship with Washington.That could appeal to supporters of separation. But it would also mean negotiating as a much smaller entity with a vastly larger neighbour.The oil problem: Getting it outThere is another practical problem that could become central to any serious independence debate: Alberta may have the oil, but it does not have an ocean.The province is landlocked.For decades, Alberta has therefore depended on pipelines and railways to move crude to refineries and export terminals.That is why access to the Pacific has mattered so much.The Trans Mountain pipeline expansion has given Canadian oil producers greater access to Canada's west coast, allowing crude to reach markets in Asia and reducing some dependence on the US.That diversification matters to Alberta.But it does not erase the American connection.An independent Alberta would therefore have to work out new arrangements with Canada while protecting access to American and overseas markets.The oil would still have to leave Alberta somehow.How serious is the movement?The fact that the question has reached the ballot does not mean Alberta is on the verge of leaving Canada.A June Ipsos poll put support for independence at 19%, according to Reuters.That figure points to an important distinction in Alberta politics.There is a sizeable and organised group that wants separation.There is also a much broader pool of Albertans who are unhappy with Ottawa but may not want to break away from Canada.Those positions are not mutually exclusive.An Albertan can oppose federal energy policy without wanting an international border.They can support more provincial control over taxation without wanting a new currency.They can favour tougher immigration rules without wanting a new country.And they can believe Alberta contributes too much to the federation while still wanting to remain Canadian.That middle ground could prove critical as the debate develops.October 19 is not Alberta's independence dayWhatever happens on October 19, Alberta will not wake up the next morning as a newly independent country.The referendum itself is non-binding. A vote to begin the legal process would be the start of another political and constitutional fight, not a declaration of independence.There would still have to be a future binding referendum. There would be negotiations. There would be disputes over money, borders, resources, Indigenous rights, trade and the division of federal assets and liabilities.Even a vote against beginning the process would not make Alberta's grievances disappear.The province would remain Canada's largest oil producer. Ottawa and Edmonton would continue to argue over resources and jurisdiction. Alberta would remain economically intertwined with the US.And Donald Trump would still be sitting just south of the border, talking about a “51st State”.That is what makes Alberta's independence debate so unusual.For decades, the province's political anger was aimed primarily east, at Ottawa.Now there is another direction to look. And that is south.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
articles.summary: Princess Diana's brother describes press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and says he saw his sister cry "tears o...
articles.body:
Diana's brother says Harry and Meghan face 'cancerous' press like his sister

Earl Spencer has told the BBC the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's treatment at the hands of the media has "echoes" of what happened to his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.

He described press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and said it would be "beholden on people to learn from Diana's example".

The Sussexes, who recently returned to the UK from California six years after stepping back from royal duties, have been repeatedly critical of the media.

It comes after the BBC reported on Friday how Earl Spencer says he was "telling the truth" when he claimed King Charles said people would forget Diana "soon enough" in a phone call in the days after her death .

Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face.

"If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied.

"And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example.

"I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."

He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".

Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan.

He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."

Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997.

In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness".

His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.

They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.

Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".

Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".

In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.

In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.

Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles.

That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".

Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles.

"It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".

However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.

Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

articles.title: DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE: Is Donald Trump's Greenland deal crucial for America and Nato to counter Russia and China in the Arctic circle?
articles.summary: US News: Explore how Donald Trump's Greenland deal may reshape NATO's military strategy and strengthen defenses against Russian and Chinese threats in the Arctic.
articles.body: There are shows that age well, and then there is Yes, Minister, which, in its plots, contains almost everything you need to learn about bureaucracy, democracy, the civil service, inter-departmental committees and even life itself. The BBC show was deemed so realistic that Margaret Thatcher was a huge fan and even appeared alongside Paul Eddington and Nigel Hawthorne in a special sketch. Now, anyone who has watched the show knows that Sir Humphrey Appleby doesn’t goof up often, but when he does, it is usually a doozy.And Yes, Minister, like the works of Franz Kafka, often feels less like satire of its own time and more like an unnervingly accurate portrait of the future.Take, for example, the plot of The Skeleton in the Cupboar, where it emerges that, in the years after the Second World War, a junior civil servant had bungled the lease of a Scottish island on which the War Office had built a military base and associated installations. Thirty years later, the lease was expiring and the government discovered that, thanks to the original agreement, the entire lot — some £40 million worth — would revert to the owner.”The junior civil servant, of course, turns out to have been Sir Humphrey Appleby, who is reduced to a blubbering idiot shouting about “foreign powers”, MI5 and MI6 before giving perhaps the most loquaciously verbose admission of guilt ever committed to television.And while that might seem like an amusing bureaucratic obscurity from an old BBC sitcom, reality has a way of becoming a Yes, Minister re-run. The recent talk of Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales potentially ‘leaving’ the United Kingdom — coupled with the new Greenland deal between Denmark, Greenland, and the United States — makes the episode look almost accidentally prophetic.But to understand why all of this matters without reading a thousand think-tank pieces in gobbledygook, one needs to understand a few things, starting with a rather innocuous-sounding acronym: GIUK.Mind the GIUK gapThe acronym stands for the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap, which might sound like an obscure inter-departmental committee but refers to particular geography. As this map below shows, it refers to the empty spaces between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. Now, Moscow’s Northern Fleet is concentrated on Russia’s Kola Peninsula, ergo any Russian submarine coming out of the Arctic and Norwegian seas would have to negotiate a series of passages formed by Greenland, Iceland and the UK before it can operate in the wider North Atlantic.Ergo, the GIUK gap is a gateway that Nato has spent decades watching. During the Cold War, detecting Soviet submarines was one of the West’s favourite maritime obsessions, and while the Soviet Union eventually disappeared, that obsession and Russia’s submarines didn’t.At the end of the day, Nato is fundamentally a transatlantic alliance.In the event of a hypothetical war in Europe, the US would have to move men, ammunition and other bits and pieces of its great military complex to reinforce the continent. Ergo, any opponent of America or Europe would do well to make those sea lanes as hazardous as possible, while Nato wouldn’t want any Russian subs lurking around and making a dash into the Atlantic.The British also hold Gibraltar, overlooking the western entrance to the Mediterranean, giving the UK a strategically important position at another major maritime chokepoint. Norway has an Atlantic-facing coast, while Spain, France and Portugal also possess direct Atlantic access from continental Europe.All this makes the GIUK gap, free access to the North Atlantic and Scotland’s geography essential to any Nato defence plans.From Russia-China with loveNow come the antagonists: a rejuvenated Russia under Putin, certainly more so than at any point since the fall of the USSR, and a boisterous China.Russia is already a great Arctic power with a powerful military. The Kola Peninsula is the heart of Russia’s Northern Fleet, which protects Moscow’s strategic nuclear forces. It’s also the base from where Russian submarines can approach the GIUK gap and, in case of any conflict involving Europe, would be a hotbed of activity.Nato argues that Moscow has increased military activity in that region and that the Arctic Sentry multi-domain military activity is in response to that growing presence.Ergo, Russia’s problem is navigating the gap to reach the North Atlantic, while Nato's is to detect and contain it.Now, Beijing isn’t in the same boat, literally or proverbially.While China might call itself a “near-Arctic state”, Beijing’s influence is more monetary than military, and it’s an important region for shipping, minerals and infra.In 2018, Beijing talked of a Polar Silk Road, encouraging Chinese companies to invest in infrastructure for Arctic shipping routes. Greenland, too, is very rich in minerals, while Beijing — much to the chagrin of America and Europe — is remarkably adept at rare-earth refining.In 2024, US and Danish officials had to pressure the developer of Greenland’s huge Tanbreez rare-earth project not to sell to China-linked buyers.Both China and Russia present different problems for the US and Europe in the area: Moscow wants to break out in case of a war, while China wants to get in to make more moolah, have more influence and ensure that, in case of a war, it doesn’t get locked out. And Greenland is essential to all the would-be belligerents.The Greenland situationGreenland was a Danish colony from 1721 to 1953 before being incorporated into the Kingdom of Denmark. Over time, Greenlanders wanted more independence, so Home Rule arrived in 1979, giving Nuuk a lot more say, which increased with 2009’s Greenland Self-Government Act.And now the Uncle Sam bit. When Nazi Germany occupied Denmark in 1940, a year later, the USA reached an agreement with the Danish ambassador to allow Washington to use Greenland as a military base while formally recognising Danish sovereignty.Long before Trump arrived on the scene, the US even considered the most Trumpian of solutions: buying it in 1946–47 before settling for using it as a long-term military base. The Americans ultimately settled for something more practical than buying Greenland: making sure they could use it.The 1951 US-Denmark Defence Agreement gave Washington long-term military access, while today Pituffik Space Base, formerly Thule Air Base, remains a crucial American missile-warning and space-surveillance outpost in the Arctic.The 2026 agreement, announced on September 18 and expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly before going through the necessary parliamentary procedures, reportedly gives the US permanent access, basing and overflight rights, prevents non-NATO countries from establishing military bases and restricts sensitive investments from potential adversaries.The full treaty obviously isn’t public, but that’s the gist: Washington wants its military position insulated irrespective of whether Greenland is independent or remains with Denmark.And that brings us to the Scottish side of the problem.The Divided Kingdom problemNow we come to the other part of the GIUK gap and why some brows are furrowed. Scotland isn’t Greenland, and the UK in particular is not a single indivisible block, but the emergence of political parties that want to consider independence from the UK, like Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland, the Scottish National Party in Scotland and Plaid Cymru in Wales, does cause a little consternation. Even Trump stoked the fire, saying he would “love” to see a united Ireland, later reiterating that he would like it to happen sooner rather than later, while declining to discuss Scottish independence “yet”.This doesn’t mean the UK just becomes England next Tuesday, but it does create a slight problem because Scotland is crucial to the British realm’s defence and any talk of Scottish freedom makes Westminster queasy.RAF Lossiemouth in north-east Scotland hosts Britain’s P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, which are specialised planes that hunt and track submarines. Faslane, on the Clyde near Glasgow, is also the main base for the Royal Navy’s submarine fleet.Together, Lossiemouth and Faslane are the core of Britain’s current ability to police its end of the GIUK gap. A House of Commons report stated that Britain’s ability to project military assets into the North Atlantic and High North is based primarily on those two assets, making them essential to both Britain and Nato.In a hypothetical scenario, take Scotland out of the defence map and both start to look vulnerable.And then there is Trident, a name anyone who has seen Yes, Prime Minister will be familiar with — something that (now) PM Jim Hacker didn't cancel so he could get a cook at 10 Downing Street.Now, Faslane is also home to Britain’s Vanguard-class ballistic-missile submarines that carry the Trident II D5 missiles armed with British nuclear warheads.Ergo, Trident is the UK’s sea-based nuclear deterrent: since 1969, Britain has had a policy of keeping at least one nuclear-armed ballistic-missile submarine at sea at all times, giving it the option to retaliate in case the UK is attacked. Nearby Coulport hosts the nuclear warheads that are loaded into the Trident missile system, and together Faslane and Coulport underpin Britain’s at-sea nuclear deterrent.All that could be lost at sea, proverbially at least, in the space of some hypothetical Scottish bid for independence. The Scottish Government says an independent Scotland would seek Nato membership and maintain strong relations with the rest of the UK, but it also wants to remove nuclear weapons from Scottish soil as quickly and safely as possible.Now, hypothetically, that means Scotland can remain pro-Nato, pro-American and pro-West, and Edinburgh could still allow allied aircraft, ships and submarines to use Scottish facilities and continue helping Nato monitor the North Atlantic, but with one caveat: on its own terms.London could no longer automatically exercise sovereign control over the territory that contains its most important military infrastructure. That doesn’t mean the Royal Navy gets an eviction notice overnight, but there would suddenly be lots of things to discuss between London, Edinburgh and Nato. Scotland’s own proposals envisage Faslane as a conventional naval base but explicitly exclude nuclear weapons.In the past, Moscow has tried to influence the region, with credible open-source commentary suggesting Russia undertook campaigns during the 2014 independence referendum. In simpler terms, Moscow might not be making Mel Gibson shout freedom, but will certainly enjoy anything that complicates Britain’s nuclear arrangements or roils Nato's current access at one end of the GIUK gap.In a situation like this, the Greenland pact is crucial: the more uncertainty Nato faces at the British end of the GIUK gap, the more certainty America would want in Greenland. No Western force wants two strategically important pieces of geography to become politically complicated.And that brings us to the most important question:is it entirely coincidental that Washington moved with such alacrity to agree a deal with Denmark and Greenland to future-proof its military position in Greenland when another part of the GIUK Gap looks more vulnerable than ever?No causality can be drawn, and, as history shows from Afghanistan to Vietnam to Korea, strategic geography lasts much longer than political arrangements.The irony here — and Trump has truly dismantled the post-WWII world order — is that while America is trying to make US access in Greenland survive constitutional change, its President is cheerfully prodding the constitutional integrity of another Nato ally by openly supporting Irish reunification and not closing the door when asked about Scotland. None of that means America wants revenge on its former colonial overlord, but it does make for an odd juxtaposition: Washington is planning for borders to matter less militarily while its President keeps reminding everybody how politically movable they can be.The Sir Humphrey problemThere’s also the small bureaucratic oversight that started this entire piece. In Yes, Minister, the junior bureaucrat fails to realise that the base will be governed by Scottish law, not English law.In real life, we have the 1978 Vienna Convention on state succession, which protects territorial treaty obligations after a change of sovereignty but specifically excludes agreements relating to foreign military bases. Neither Denmark nor the US is a party to that Convention, but the underlying principle remains that a commitment by a sovereign state isn’t like Salman Khan’s: it can change.Perhaps the Greenland pact is simply an attempt to ensure the least disruption. At the moment, policing this end of the GIUK gap lies more heavily with Britain — Faslane and Coulport underpin Britain’s nuclear deterrent — and any constitutional rupture would create two specific problems: continuity of Nato operations and Britain’s nuclear posture.Since the Cold War, Nato has slept peacefully knowing that Denmark included Greenland and Britain had Scotland. But recent developments raise a question: what if that reality changed tomorrow?And that perhaps explains why Washington is so keen to ensure that Greenland is wired in properly, because it cannot guarantee Europe’s political borders but can try to ensure that constitutional uncertainty doesn’t become a strategic opening for Russia or China.Perhaps that is the real lesson of the Greenland pact. Those who fail to learn from history are condemned to repeat it. Humphrey’s mistake was forgetting that distinction until the lease ran out. Washington appears determined not to make the same mistake. After all, as Littlefinger pointed out: chaos is a ladder, and Washington is hellbent on ensuring Russia or China doesn’t get a foot on that ladder.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Washington couple spent nearly two decades and $50 million creating a resort-style retreat on 2.3 acres of Lake Washington; the two-home waterfront compound now asks $71 million
articles.summary: News News: Dwayne Clark and his wife, Terese Clark, are selling their two-home property on Lake Washington, along with the adjacent land, for $71 million, accord.
articles.body: Dwayne Clark and his wife, Terese Clark, are selling their two-home property on Lake Washington, along with the adjacent land, for $71 million, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. If the 2.3-acre waterfront compound sells near the asking price, it could set a record for Pacific Northwest residential real estate. Last year, Jeff Bezos sold a mansion in the neighbourhood for a record-breaking price.Lake Washington home is up for saleIn 2008, the Clarks purchased a 1.2-acre waterfront compound in Hunts Point, Bellevue, Washington, for $4.9 million. They tore down the old cottage on the property and constructed a roughly 9,600-square-foot residence. About a decade later, they bought an adjacent 1.12-acre property for roughly $8 million, where they built a second home designed specifically as a wellness retreat.The couple had a unique vision for their home. Dwayne, 67, founder and CEO of senior-living company Áegis Living, and Terese, 66, a retired trauma nurse, wanted to create a space that reflected their shared love of travel, wellness and Italy. People raised eyebrows when they built a piazza, an open courtyard enclosed on four sides and a feature of Italian architecture, at their waterfront home in Bellevue. The structure didn’t make sense to some, as it is in one of Washington state's rainiest neighbourhoods. “People said, ‘No one has piazzas in Seattle,’” Terese told the WSJ. But they did it anyway. The partly sheltered space allows them to enjoy the outdoors even when it is raining, and according to Dwayne, the piazza creates its own warmer ‘microclimate’. The couple's affection for Italy drove many of the design choices across their Hunts Point property. Over nearly 20 years, they acquired furnishings and décor from their travels, layering the European aesthetic into what would become their waterfront sanctuary. Over the two decades, the couple has invested about $50 million. “What we’ve tried to do is create our own Four Seasons resort,” Dwayne said.Despite putting a lot of effort into their waterfront homes, the Clarks are now moving to a sunnier climate. They are hoping to relocate to Arizona, and Dwayne also plans to retire from his role this year. They have listed their Bellevue home for sale.If the sale closes near the $71 million asking price, it would establish a record for the region, listing agents Jay Kipp of Realogics Sotheby’s International Realty and Haleh Clapp of Compass told the publication. Jeff Bezos sold his Hunts Point mansion last year for $63 million, Kipp pointed out.What the buyer getsThe buyer gets 2.3 acres of Lake Washington waterfront with two Mediterranean-style residences connected by a bridge over a koi pond. The main house spans roughly 9,600 square feet, with three bedrooms, a piazza and rooms filled with Italian furnishings collected over decades. The second property, completed in 2024, functions as a dedicated wellness retreat with indoor and outdoor pools, a separate stone cottage and an attached garage that doubles as a ballroom for entertaining. Two private docks provide direct access to the lake. The entire compound arrives turnkey, with curated décor and design elements sourced exclusively from Italy. According to Dwayne, these two houses were a ‘labour of love’.Meanwhile, the Clarks also own a beachfront home in Santa Barbara, California, which they have listed for $44.999 million. They plan to relocate to Arizona, where they can pursue an active outdoor lifestyle with more consistent sunshine.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: A Washington couple claims 'Microsoft data centre conspiracy'; says spent nearly $300,000 to build a home on their family land; state now demands they surrender 44 acres
articles.summary: Tech News News: A Washington couple claims they have been caught in what they describe as a “Microsoft data centre conspiracy” after spending nearly $300,000 trying t.
articles.body: A Washington couple claims they have been caught in what they describe as a “Microsoft data centre conspiracy” after spending nearly $300,000 trying to build a home on their family land. Tyler and Wendy Chambers own 66 acres in Chelan County and say they completed multiple studies and regulatory requirements before being told they would need to permanently set aside 44.2 acres to move ahead with construction.​According to a report by AG Web, the couple and their real estate broker, Jeff Hallman, have questioned why the requirements applied to their property while Microsoft built a data centre about 10 miles away. Hallman specifically compares the amount of earthmoving involved in the two projects. However, the claims come from Chambers and Hallman, who have criticised the county and state over the property dispute.​How the property dispute beganChambers, 59, and his wife bought three tax parcels totalling 66 acres in 2021. The property, located outside Wenatchee, was zoned residential and had access to power, water and roads. Chambers said he planned to build a home and pole barn and eventually allow his children or grandchildren to build on the property.He says he completed several checks before starting construction, including geological, soil, survey and engineering assessments. In fall 2021, he received approval to proceed from Chelan County Community Development Director Jim Brown.However, people later complained about earthmoving on the property. Chambers said a county investigation initially found the complaint to be unfounded.​On October 5, 2021, Chelan County Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Marcus Foster wrote: “…The county has investigated the complaint and determined it is unfounded … Unless circumstances change, the county will not be taking further action in this manner.”​More studies followedThe situation changed after Brown left his position and Deanna Walter became director of Chelan County Community Development in 2022. Chambers said a stop-work order followed, after which the county requested additional reports and studies.According to Chambers, these included assessments involving stormwater, spotted owls, golden eagles, deer, shrubsteppe, geotechnical conditions and mitigation.“Literally, we even had to do a study to make sure we weren’t hurting spotted owls,” Chambers says. “Also, just as another countless example, there’s a drainage ditch nearby and I had to get a study to prove it wasn’t fish-bearing. It was all crazy, but we kept believing each request was the final one and each hurdle was the last we’d have to jump.”​Chambers says he eventually spent almost $300,000 on regulatory requirements and professional reports.​Why Chambers compares his case with Microsoft​The biggest dispute came when Chambers says he was required to permanently set aside 44.2 acres, or about two-thirds of his property, as mitigation before he could build.​Chambers and Hallman allege that the requirement was inconsistent with how a nearby Microsoft data centre project was treated. They point to a Microsoft project roughly 10 miles away and claim the company moved substantially more earth while being asked to set aside less land. These comparisons are allegations by Chambers and Hallman; the material provided does not independently establish that Microsoft received preferential treatment or that the two cases were connected.​“About 10 miles away, Microsoft is building a data center. Microsoft has moved 500,000 cubic yards of dirt. Tyler’s guessed amount of 1,000 is 1/500th of that—like $2 on a $1,000 bill. So how much land was Microsoft asked to set aside? Substantially less than Tyler. Still think conspiracies aren’t real?” he claimed.​Chambers also asks why neighbouring properties didn't face the same requirement.​“Guess how many of Tyler’s neighbouring homes faced a wildlife habitat easement?” Chambers asks. “None. The people beside him are immune from this regulatory insanity. That should be a major tell for a neutral observer.”​Chambers calls demand ‘extortion’​Chambers says the prolonged dispute has caused financial and personal stress for his family.​“Extortion. Theft. Unconstitutional. My family has been through hell,” Chambers says. “If you think you own land, then check out what the bureaucracy has done on my property.”​He says the family still pays about $3,000 a month on its construction loan despite being unable to proceed with the project.​“Think how unbelievably dictatorial Chelan County’s stance is. They demand control of two-thirds of Tyler’s land—three historical tax parcels with PUD water, power, fiber and road access. In my opinion, it’s because some county leaders, behind closed doors, genuinely believe private property doesn’t exist. They think all property belongs to the state. You pay the taxes, but live by their rules, since in their unstated view it belongs to the collective. They make and change rules as needed,” he added.​Chambers says he plans to continue challenging the restrictions and still intends to build a home on the property.​Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.summary: UK News: Late Princess Diana's brother, Earl Charles Spencer, said in an interview published Sunday that Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are facing media trea.
articles.body: Late Princess Diana's brother, Earl Charles Spencer, said in an interview published Sunday that Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are facing media treatment comparable to what his sister endured, and cautioned that lessons must be drawn from that era.Diana died at age 36 in a 1997 car crash in Paris while being chased by photographers on motorbikes, an event that triggered widespread public grief and prompted questions over whether the media shared blame for her death after years of splashing details of her private life across front pages."If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," Spencer told the BBC."And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example"."I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life", he said.Harry, the younger of Diana's two sons, and Meghan had pointed to the effects of what they described as a toxic media environment as a factor in their decision to step back from royal duties and relocate to the United States in 2020.They subsequently took legal action against a large part of the British tabloid press, achieving mixed results, before returning to live in Britain in August.Spencer has drawn global attention over the past week following the serialization of his book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," in the Daily Mail, in which he claims that Diana's former husband, now King Charles, sounded "giddily elated" in the hours following her death.In response, the palace stated that the king "is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."The book's release, along with Harry and Meghan's return to Britain, presents a further difficulty for the king, who continues to receive articles.title: Nearly 20 years after Dreyer’s Ice Cream CEO T. Gary Rogers bought 151 acres in Napa, his family discovered an 1887 winery hidden on the property; they planted vineyards, built a home, and the estate now asks $35 million
articles.summary: Real Estate News: A vineyard property in Napa Valley, featuring an 1887 winery that Ellen DeGeneres once had her eyes on, is on the market. The 151-acre property in St .
articles.body: A vineyard property in Napa Valley, featuring an 1887 winery that Ellen DeGeneres once had her eyes on, is on the market. The 151-acre property in St Helena, California, is listed for $35 million, according to a report by Mansion Global. The seller is artist Matt Rogers, the son of the late T. Gary Rogers, the former CEO of Dreyer’s Ice Cream and former chairman of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. La Herradura Ranch is no longer a working ranch, but it still retains much of its historic character, with about 25 acres of vineyards, a private lake and several structures, including a recently built main house and the restored 1887 stone winery.A hidden ghost wineryAbout 20 years ago, Gary Rogers bought the vineyard. He already owned the neighbouring ranch and wanted to combine the two properties to own a square mile of land, Matt told the outlet.After the property was divided, Rogers asked his son Matt, who lived there, to prepare the remaining land for sale. That’s when Matt discovered something unusual. He discovered a hidden 1887 stone winery. The building had been obscured for decades, hidden beneath a 1950s ranch house with an addition that came down around 2008. Little documentation existed about its origins, but the Rogers family traced it back to Mountain Cove Winery, a small vertical operation that likely produced jug wine and supplied local churches during Napa’s early wine era.On Friday, September 18, Erin Lail of Coldwell Banker Brokers of the Valley listed it on the market.“It’s a beautiful, gorgeous firestone cathedral. When you open the big steel doors and play some music and have some friends over, it’s just such a unique, special place. You can just feel the spirit of the valley,” Matt told the publication.Around 2008, the 4,000-sq.-ft. addition to the winery was torn down, revealing the original rustic stone exterior. The structure was restored with new electrical, plumbing, floors and doors, according to the property’s website. The new space can accommodate roughly 100 people, and the Rogers family has hosted everything from fundraisers to comedy shows within those stone walls. The space became less about wine production and more about creating moments, a versatile backdrop for the social calendar of Napa’s wine country elite.After the restoration, the family decided to sell La Herradura, and the property grabbed the attention of Ellen DeGeneres. “Our big exciting day was when Ellen DeGeneres and Portia came up to look at it. They didn’t like the fact that there was cattle on the property,” Matt said. The couple were vegans at the time.What the buyer getsBeyond the restored winery, the property has been substantially developed in recent years. A new main house was completed in 2024. The nearly 2,500-sq.-ft. home has an open-plan layout, with three bedrooms and three bathrooms. A small cabin sits along the property’s private lake, outfitted with bunks, a fireplace, indoor plumbing and an outdoor shower, serving as a getaway spot for fishing and swimming.“You could spend the night and camp out or use it as a getaway. It’s a very rough little fishing cabin, but it makes using the lake much more accessible,” Matt told the outlet. The property also has a two-bedroom cottage north of the main house, along with another, slightly larger two-bedroom residence.Matt and his wife, Amy, redid the entire vineyard. They replanted the vines in 2020, along with a new drainage system. The vineyard now grows Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc, with half an acre reserved for Sauvignon Blanc.“Originally, it was the party house. This was supposed to be a buy-it-and-flip. If my dad were still alive and he was still promoting these events we used to do, that would probably keep it going, but it just doesn’t make sense anymore,” Matt said.Rogers passed away in 2017, at the age of 74.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.body: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced on Sunday that Italy will ban face coverings including burqa and hijab in schools and impose a limit on the number of foreign students allowed per classroom, speaking at a youth event hosted by her Brothers of Italy party."A measure will soon be presented to a Cabinet meeting to legally establish a maximum number of foreign students per class. articles.title: Meet Ameya Kharade, the 17-year-old Nashua student whose $1,800 brain-reading system aims to turn brain activity into speech at implant-like speeds without surgery
articles.summary: US News: For someone who can speak, putting a thought into words is almost effortless. For millions of people living with conditions such as ALS, severe stroke.
articles.body: For someone who can speak, putting a thought into words is almost effortless. For millions of people living with conditions such as ALS, severe stroke or paralysis, that simple act can become impossible even when the mind remains fully active. At 17, Nashua, New Hampshire, student Ameya Kharade is working on a way to close that gap without putting a device inside the brain. According to a report by Newsnet Los Angeles, his project, called HALO-Vox, is a brain-computer interface designed to translate brain activity into speech far more quickly than conventional non-invasive systems. What makes the project particularly striking is its price. Kharade developed and tested the system using about $1,800 worth of consumer electroencephalography hardware rather than an expensive surgical implant. Scroll down to read the details.A personal learningAccording to Barron Prize Winners website data, Ameya’s work is rooted in his close family member’s loss of speech following a stroke when Ameya was seven. He could see in his relative’s eyes that his mind was intact, but his voice was gone. Refusing to accept that, Ameya applied the neuroscience research he’s done since age 13 to solving the speech problem. Working alone in his garage for more than six hours each day for a year, he taught himself the mathematics of information theory, developed a sixty-page theory paper, created the algorithms, wrote the code, and ran the human trials. He discovered that for decades, the entire field working to restore speech had been trying to decode letters when they should have been decoding “intent” itself. In over 100 human trial sessions, HALO-Vox’s built-in safety system has never put unintended words in a speaker’s mouth. Ameya has open-sourced his system so anyone can use it and has filed a patent to protect its accessibility. Ameya is now bringing this technology to the whole world. He co-founded Lucen to put brain-computer interfaces within reach of anyone, without millions of dollars and without brain surgery. Extending HALO-Vox, he and his team are building the foundational technology and physics to make that possible. “I’ve learned that persistence isn’t about confidence,” says Ameya. “It’s about being committed enough that giving up isn’t something you can live with.”A different way to read intentCurrent non-invasive brain-computer interfaces can be painfully slow, with conventional systems often requiring users to construct messages letter by letter. Surgical implants can deliver much faster communication, but they involve brain surgery and can cost well over $100,000. According to Society for Science data, Kharade took a different approach. Instead of treating communication as a process of spelling out individual characters, HALO-Vox attempts to identify the underlying intent of a person's brain activity.In testing involving 111 randomized, counterbalanced trials, the system reached 65 words per minute, compared with 3 words per minute for a conventional speller using the same hardware. The results represented a roughly 20-fold improvement in speed. The system also reduced the time required to produce a message, with testing showing an average of 10.7 seconds compared with 242.2 seconds for the conventional approach.Focusing on meaning, not sentence lengthKharade's research points toward a different measure of communication efficiency. His system appeared to respond more strongly to ambiguity in a person's intended message than to the length of the sentence itself. That distinction led him to develop what he calls the Six Laws of Intent Resolution, a framework based on information theory that describes how communication systems can extract more meaning from limited signals. The idea could extend beyond speech. Kharade argues that the same principle could eventually improve other bandwidth-limited technologies, including prosthetics and existing brain-computer interfaces.A project with a wider purposeAs per the Newsnet Los Angeles report, Kharade's work has also earned recognition beyond the laboratory. He is among the 2026 winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which honors 25 young people between the ages of 8 and 18 for significant contributions to people and the planet. For Kharade, the technology is ultimately aimed at a basic human need: giving people who cannot physically speak another way to communicate. If HALO-Vox can continue to demonstrate its early results, the project could offer a glimpse of a future where sophisticated brain-computer communication does not necessarily require a surgeon, a six-figure price tag or years of specialized equipment.Image Courtesy: Barron Prize Winners Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: More than 1,300 tonnes of old concrete pipes are being dropped into the Gulf of Mexico to create a series of artificial reefs off the coast of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida. The project uses three million pounds of recycled concrete culverts to create three separate underwater habitats. Each site will receive about 500 tons of heavy material. The project is being led by Okaloosa County’s Natural Resources Team, along with the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. As reported by regional TV station WJHG, the project is the second major deployment of Florida's Coastal Corridor, a statewide conservation program designed to connect marine habitats along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.Heavy materials dropped off East PassContractors are placing the concrete culverts in approved offshore areas about four to eight nautical miles from East Pass, according to information from the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida. The material is being placed at depths of about 68 to 74 feet below the surface. Workers are arranging the culverts in dense groups to create tall structures on the ocean floor. The hollow concrete pipes provide shelter for marine animals that have few hard surfaces to live on across the Gulf's mostly sandy seabed. The deployment began in mid-September 2026 and is expected to continue through November 2026.Supporting marine life and local fisheriesOnce the concrete settles on the seafloor, its hard surfaces give algae, sponges, barnacles, and soft corals places to attach and grow. These organisms then provide food and shelter for crabs, baitfish, and larger species such as grouper and snapper. State wildlife officials said these structures can help support healthy fish populations in the region. “Thoughtfully planned artificial reefs can play an important role in conserving and enhancing marine habitat while supporting the long-term health of Florida's fisheries,” said Roger Young, Executive Director of the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, in an official statement released by the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida. “Projects like this bring together sound science, careful site selection, durable materials, and strong local partnerships to create habitat that supports marine life and helps sustain healthy marine resources for generations to come.”Statewide network expands to the PanhandleThe Okaloosa County project is part of a larger effort to connect underwater habitats across Florida. The first official deployment under the Coastal Corridor program took place off Naples in early September 2026, when prefabricated reef units were placed underwater. Local officials said these regional projects need to work together to protect marine species that move across the Gulf of Mexico. “These collaborations are necessary to continue the statewide effort to improve habitat for marine life in the Gulf,” said Okaloosa County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin in a statement published by the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida. “We appreciate the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida for choosing Destin-Fort Walton Beach to add to our already vibrant artificial reef system.”Economic and recreational benefitsThe new reefs are expected to provide more places for charter boat operators, recreational fishermen, and scuba divers. Okaloosa County has one of the more active artificial reef programs in the United States, managing hundreds of approved sites that include sunken tugboats, military targets, and concrete reef structures. By placing strong, long-lasting concrete culverts in accessible waters near the coast, local officials hope to spread fishing and diving activity across more locations. This could reduce pressure on natural reef areas while creating new destinations for eco-tourism. The Coastal Corridor program plans to continue habitat restoration along Florida's coast after the Destin-Fort Walton Beach project. Future work will include mangrove planting, seagrass restoration, and more offshore reef projects through the end of the year.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘What are you other than English?’ Former UK PM Rishi Sunak slams defining Britishness by skin colour
articles.summary: UK News: Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak defends British identity, asserting that skin colour should not determine nationality. He highlights the importance of integration and shared culture in a multi-ethnic society.
articles.body: Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak has warned against equating skin colour with nationality, saying people born and raised in England should not have their English or British identity questioned because they are not white.Writing on X on Sunday, Sunak said his Cowdrey Lecture at the Marylebone Cricket Club on Thursday had prompted him to reflect on cricket's place in British life and the country's debate over identity and integration.Race and British identitySunak said Britain had built a multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy but warned that this achievement was under strain. He identified immigration and Islamism as challenges, while also highlighting what he described as a growing tendency to associate race with nationality.He pointed to online discussions after he left office questioning whether he was English because he was a "brown Hindu". Sunak described this as a "reverse Tebbit test", in which a person's support for England would no longer determine whether they were accepted as English because their skin colour would disqualify them.He also recalled footage from an election campaign in which someone called him a racial slur, saying the incident was shocking because such abuse had been unusual during his political career.Immigration and integration debate Sunak argued that concerns about immigration can coexist with opposition to defining Britishness through race. He said he supported a high bar for legal migration and had spent much of his premiership pursuing the deportation of asylum seekers to Rwanda."It is entirely possible to want a radical reduction in immigration and a far more robust approach to integration, and still totally reject the attempt to turn Britishness into a DNA test," he wrote."If you're born and brought up in England and view it as home, what are you other than English?"The former PM said denying people their Englishness or Britishness because of their skin colour risked creating alienation and a two-tier society.Cricket and shared identitySunak also pointed to cricket as a way of bringing different communities together. He said the sport connects people from different ethnic backgrounds, citing the shared interest in cricket among his largely white rural constituents in the Yorkshire Dales and British Asian children in Bradford.He argued that England teams in which children from different backgrounds can see themselves could help reinforce a shared sense of belonging."We must all be on the same side, cheering for the same team," Sunak wrote, adding that Britain should not allow race to be reintroduced into its politics.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: MAGA brown-out: For Indian Trump acolytes, citizenship comes with an asterisk
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: For years, Indian-origin conservatives in the Trump orbit have been comforting themselves that race doesn't matter,.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: For years, Indian-origin conservatives in the Trump orbit have been comforting themselves that race doesn't matter, ideology does. They are now discovering a rather inconvenient footnote: in the MAGA world, you can pass the ideological exam and still fail the race test and dinner evaluation.Trump’s Chandigarh-born legal luminary Harmeet Dhillon’s effort to portray herself as all-American by posting a photo of a beef dinner has invited ridicule from MAGA trolls, as has conservative Dinesh D’Souza’s attempt to defend his daughter from racist attacks by telling MAGA exclusionists that her mother is white. Ohio-governor aspirant Vivek Ramaswamy and Trump’s former UN envoy Nikki Haley, at various points, found themselves having to demonstrate that they are American enough.Democrats and liberals have of course experienced this to an even greater degree. Washington lawmaker Pramila Jayapal, who has heard the “go back to India” call from MAGA extremists for years, has faced death threats, including reporting a man carrying a loaded Glock outside her Seattle home. Some have responded cheekily. Asked last week to “take your curry and go home” by a MAGA Republican, Illinois Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi clapped back: “I’m staying. So is the curry. America is my home. No bigot gets to decide who is American, who belongs here, or what they have for dinner. That’s the America I’ll always fight for.”Progressives are relishing the schadenfreude that comes with needling conservative Republican desis who had signed up for MAGA. “Imagine hating your brown self so much, having so little self pride or self worth, that you voluntarily and proudly tell people on the internet that your daughter’s mom is white,” liberal commentator Mehdi Hasan, himself a target of vile racist attacks from MAGA, taunted D’Souza, who has long distanced himself from his Mumbai-origins.Vivek Ramaswamy has had the longest-running version of this particular identity seminar. The Ohio Republican, self-professed Hindu son of Indian immigrants and former presidential candidate, built much of his political career attacking what he regarded as left-wing racial grievance politics. Now, running for governor of Ohio, he has encountered racial hostility from the right. His Republican primary opponent Casey Putsch has attacked him as an “Indian boy” who was merely “cosplaying an American,” invoked “blood and soil” language and questioned whether Ramaswamy was genuinely American.Ramaswamy has responded by attacking the increasingly popular notion among MAGA that “heritage Americans” have some superior claim to the country. He has also said his social-media feeds became so saturated with slurs and demands that he return to India that he quit posting personally on X and Instagram. The irony is rich: Ramaswamy once argued that race should not determine American identity. He is now explaining that principle to people who apparently believe ancestry should.Nikki Haley encountered an earlier version of the same contradiction. The former South Carolina governor and UN ambassador, born in South Carolina to Sikh immigrants from Punjab, was told by conservative commentator Ann Coulter during Haley’s 2023 presidential campaign to “go back to your own country.” Coulter coupled the remark with references to India’s supposed cow and rat worship. Even Trump repeatedly mocked Haley's birth name, Nimarata, during the 2024 Republican primary campaign.And then there is the curious case of the man married to an Indian-American woman. Vice President JD Vance's wife, Usha Vance, was targeted by white-nationalist Nick Fuentes and others after Vance became Trump's running mate in 2024. Fuentes attacked the couple's interracial marriage and invoked “replacement” rhetoric over Usha's Indian ancestry. Vance later responded to continuing attacks on his wife by saying critics could “eat s---.”This year, Usha has again become a racial subtext in an argument involving Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. After Vance invoked his grandfather while criticising El-Sayed's views on Islam, El-Sayed snarkily asked whether Vance would take Usha “back in time to meet Papaw,” invoking the way grandfathers are referred to in the south.There is something almost wonderfully American about the absurdity of it all: immigrants and their children being asked to prove they belong by people whose own ancestors once had to prove they belonged. Harmeet plates beef, Dinesh wheels out the white wife, Vivek rolls out the Ohio birth certificate, and Nikki goes to church. And yet the MAGA bouncer at the door keeps asking the same question: “But are you really American?”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
